title: Dirty OCR Is Not Noise. It Is a Tilt.
summary: A cultural-analytics result almost always terminates in a frequency: the share of tokens in some lexicon, the prevalence of a topic, entities per million words, the cosine between two decade centroids. And almost always the optical...
body:
A cultural-analytics result almost always terminates in a frequency: the share of tokens in some lexicon, the prevalence of a topic, entities per million words, the cosine between two decade centroids. And almost always the optical character recognition is disposed of in one sentence — mean character error rate was four per cent, low-quality pages were dropped — after which the frequencies are handled as though they had been measured rather than inferred.

Those two moves are incompatible, for a reason sharper than "noisy data give noisy answers." Character-level error does not perturb a distribution over word types symmetrically. It removes types at a rate depending on how many characters they contain and which glyphs those are, and that rate is a function of the scan, the typeface, the paper stock, and therefore the decade. The corruption is aligned with the axis along which humanities questions are asked. What survives digitization is not a noisy copy of the frequency vector but a systematically reweighted one — and the reweighting moves when the digitization moves.

## The errors got better, and less visible

The error structure changed underneath the field while the aggregate numbers improved. Vesalainen and colleagues compared a dedicated OCR transformer (TrOCR) against a general-purpose vision–language model on line-level eighteenth-century English, and found the VLM achieved lower CER and WER and greater robustness to degraded input while exhibiting what they call [selective linguistic regularization and orthographic normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14524) — silently rewriting historically meaningful forms into conventional ones. TrOCR held orthographic fidelity better but propagated errors in cascades.

That is a bad trade for measurement, and the opposite of what the aggregate metric reports. Classical OCR failed loudly: the long-s rendered as *f*, broken ligatures, tokens that hit no dictionary. Digital humanities built its quality-control apparatus on that signature — garbage-token ratios, dictionary lookup rates, unknown-word proportions. A decoder with a language-model prior fails quietly instead, producing fluent in-vocabulary text that is wrong. Every heuristic the field uses to detect dirty OCR is blind by construction to that failure mode, and a lower CER buys an error you cannot find.

The infrastructure pulls the same direction. The [HIPE-OCRepair 2026 competition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08143) on LLM-assisted post-correction defines its benchmark with retrieval-oriented normalization that deliberately abstracts away orthographic variation. Defensible for search; it optimizes away exactly what a historical linguist measures.

## Attenuation is the wrong default

When a quantitative social scientist hears "measurement error" the reflex is attenuation, and here the reflex is wrong. The classical setup has a latent regressor $w^*$ observed as $w = w^* + u$ with $u \perp w^*$ and $\mathbb{E}[u]=0$; regressing an outcome on $w$ gives $\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta = \lambda\beta$ with reliability ratio $\lambda = \sigma^2_{w^*}/(\sigma^2_{w^*}+\sigma^2_u) \in (0,1)$. The estimate shrinks toward zero — the comfortable case, where the bias is signed, bounded, and conservative, so a significant finding is significant *a fortiori*.

Two assumptions carry that conclusion and text-derived measures satisfy neither. The error must be mean-zero on the latent quantity, and it must be non-differential — independent of the analysis covariates. OCR error is a deletion channel with a type-dependent rate, so its effect on a frequency has a definite sign rather than zero mean; and its severity is a deterministic function of publication date, print shop, language, and which vendor scanned the volume, which are precisely the regressors. Differential error has no sign guarantee. It can inflate, invert, and manufacture a monotone trend from a flat one.

## Frequencies under a deletion channel

Write the channel at the level of word types. Let $f_v$ be the true relative frequency of type $v$ and $\ell_v$ its length in characters. A token of type $v$ is transcribed correctly with probability $p_v$ and otherwise becomes some other string; set aside for now the possibility that it lands on another real word. Observed counts are $\hat n_v \approx p_v n_v$, so the observed relative frequency is

$$\hat f_v ;=; \frac{p_v n_v}{\sum_u p_u n_u} ;=; f_v \cdot \frac{p_v}{\bar p}, \qquad \bar p = \sum_u f_u p_u .$$

This is the whole problem in one line: the observed frequency is the true frequency times the type's survival probability relative to the corpus average. Nothing here is mean-zero. It is a tilt toward whatever OCR finds easy.

Give $p_v$ the simplest structure. If character errors are independent at rate $\epsilon$, then $p_v = (1-\epsilon)^{\ell_v}$. Let $\delta = -\log(1-\epsilon) \approx \epsilon$, $\bar\ell = \mathbb{E}*f[\ell]$, $\sigma^2*\ell = \operatorname{Var}_f(\ell)$. A cumulant expansion gives $\bar p = \mathbb{E}*f[e^{-\delta\ell}] = \exp(-\delta\bar\ell + \tfrac12\delta^2\sigma^2*\ell + O(\delta^3))$, so

$$\log\frac{\hat f_v}{f_v} ;=; -,\delta,(\ell_v - \bar\ell) ;-; \tfrac12\delta^2\sigma^2_\ell ;+; O(\delta^3).$$

To first order, every type's log-frequency is shifted by $-\epsilon$ times its length excess over the corpus mean. Long words are suppressed exponentially in length; short words are *promoted*, because normalization has to put the mass somewhere. The second-order term is a uniform offset that cancels in any ratio.

Push it through to something reportable. Any measure linear in relative frequencies — a dictionary share, a lexicon score, a topic's marginal — has the form $m = \sum_v c_v f_v = \mathbb{E}_f[c]$. Substituting the first-order tilt,

$$\hat m ;\approx; \sum_v c_v f_v\big(1 - \epsilon(\ell_v-\bar\ell)\big) ;=; m ;-; \epsilon,\operatorname{Cov}_f(c,\ell).$$

The bias in any frequency-linear measure is the character error rate times the frequency-weighted covariance between the measure's weights and word length. That covariance is computable from your own corpus and lexicon with no ground truth at all, which makes it the cheapest diagnostic in this literature and one I have never seen reported.

For an indicator lexicon $c_v = \mathbb{1}{v \in L}$ it collapses further: $\operatorname{Cov}_f(c,\ell) = m,(\bar\ell_L - \bar\ell)$, with $\bar\ell_L$ the frequency-weighted mean length inside $L$. Writing $\Delta = \bar\ell_L - \bar\ell$,

$$\frac{\hat m}{m} ;\approx; e^{-\delta\Delta}.$$

One number: the measured share of a lexicon is wrong by a factor exponential in how much longer its words are than the corpus average. The consequence for trends follows: if $\epsilon$ varies with time,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\log\hat m ;=; \frac{d}{dt}\log m ;-; \Delta,\frac{d\epsilon}{dt}.$$

A declining error rate over a collection's timespan adds a spurious upward trend to every long-worded lexicon and a downward one to every short-worded lexicon, with slope set by $\Delta$. This is not attenuation. It is signal generated from nothing, pointing whichever way the digitization improved.

## What an engine swap does to a finding

The numbers are not small. Take $\Delta = 4.7$ characters, roughly where a Latinate or abstract-noun lexicon sits against a mean token length near 4.5 in running English prose — the polysyllabic end of the vocabulary that "abstraction," "formality," and "complexity" measures are built from.

The [American Stories](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/ffeb860479ccae44d84c0de32acd693d-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.pdf) pipeline reports, on the same Day-Per-Decade sample of Chronicling America, a CER of 0.043 for its EffOCR-Word engine against 0.106 for Tesseract and 0.170 for EasyOCR. Those are three transcriptions of one archive. Under the model, the measured lexicon share is depressed by a factor $e^{-\delta\Delta}$ of 0.81, 0.59, and 0.42 respectively. Re-OCR a collection from Tesseract to EffOCR and your abstraction measure rises 38% with no change to a single page of print. From EasyOCR it nearly doubles.

Anchor the other end on ground truth. Hill and Hengchen compared Eighteenth Century Collections Online against its keyed Text Creation Partnership counterpart, reporting mean token-level accuracy around [77%](https://academic.oup.com/dsh/article-abstract/34/4/825/5476122) for their ECCO sample. Inverting $0.77 = (1-\epsilon)^{\bar\ell}$ at $\bar\ell \approx 4.5$ — my arithmetic, and the mean length is my assumption — gives $\epsilon \approx 0.056$, hence $e^{-\delta\Delta} \approx 0.76$. A quarter of the lexicon gone, systematically, in the flagship eighteenth-century corpus.

The diagnostic is four lines:

```python
import numpy as np
def length_tilt(counts, lengths, lexicon_mask, cer):
    """counts, lengths: per-type arrays over the vocabulary."""
    f = counts / counts.sum()
    lbar = f @ lengths                          # freq-weighted mean length
    m = f[lexicon_mask].sum()
    lbar_L = (f[lexicon_mask] @ lengths[lexicon_mask]) / m
    delta_len = lbar_L - lbar                   # the quantity that matters
    d = -np.log1p(-cer)
    return delta_len, np.exp(-d * delta_len)    # (length gap, bias factor)
Run it before anything else. If `delta_len` is near zero the measure is first-order immune; if it is 3 or 4, every temporal claim you make is partly a claim about scanner quality.
```

## What to do instead

**Report $\operatorname{Cov}_f(c,\ell)$ beside every lexicon result.** It costs nothing and turns an unfalsifiable worry into a signed number.

**Run a length-matched placebo.** Construct a control lexicon matched on the frequency-weighted length distribution but semantically irrelevant to the hypothesis, and estimate the same trend on it. Whatever slope it shows is your $-\Delta,d\epsilon/dt$ term, measured without needing $\epsilon$. If the real lexicon's trend does not exceed the placebo's, there is no finding.

**Stop dropping low-quality pages.** Filtering on estimated OCR quality is selection on a variable correlated with date, region, and publisher. It does not remove the bias; it silently redefines the estimand over a subpopulation that drifts along the very axis being studied. Reweighting beats filtering: with a keyed subsample, estimate $\hat p_v$ and apply Horvitz–Thompson weights $1/\hat p_v$ to counts, targeting the right quantity instead of a cleaner wrong one.

**Borrow SIMEX.** Cook and Stefanski's simulation-extrapolation method — add known extra measurement error at levels $\lambda$, trace the estimate as a function of $\lambda$, extrapolate back to $\lambda=-1$ — suits text unusually well, because here you can actually simulate the corruption channel by injecting synthetic character noise at a known multiple of the observed rate. Fit a quadratic through $\lambda \in {0,0.5,1,1.5,2}$ and evaluate at $-1$. Twenty lines, no gold data required.

**When you do have gold data, use it properly.** The design-based supervised learning estimator of Egami and colleagues combines cheap imperfect labels with a small gold-standard subsample in a doubly robust procedure restoring asymptotic unbiasedness and honest intervals. It was written for LLM annotations, but a keyed transcription subsample is the same object — and the field has had such subsamples, TCP canonically, for two decades without using them as validation sets.

**Do not blanket-apply LLM post-correction to a measurement corpus.** Kanerva and colleagues found English CER gains that did not reach practical usefulness in Finnish; correction quality covaries with language, period, and degradation, which is the definition of differential error. Correcting non-uniformly can leave you worse off than not correcting.

## Where the model breaks

The independent-character-error assumption is false, and its failure matters. Real OCR errors cluster: a bad line, a bleed-through column, a region lost to layout failure. Clustering makes $p_v$ less steeply length-dependent at a given CER, so $-\epsilon\Delta$ is better read as an upper bound on the tilt than an estimate. Worse, region-level loss is not a tilt at all but a coverage problem, and CER is the wrong instrument for it — Bourne, Simbeye and Nockels argue that CER is undefined under page-parsing failure and decompose page-level error into parsing, recognition, and interaction components instead.

I also assumed corrupted tokens vanish. Some land on real words, and the destinations are systematically short and common, because that is where the mass is. In-flow strengthens the tilt toward short words while destroying the closed form; the qualitative direction survives, the derivation does not.

The sharpest limit is that the model describes classical OCR and the field is leaving it. A vision–language decoder recognizes words holistically under a language-model prior, so a long frequent word may be transcribed *more* reliably than a short rare one, and the governing covariate becomes corpus frequency or orthographic conventionality rather than length. The tilt does not disappear — the normalization Vesalainen and colleagues document is a tilt toward modern standard forms, worse for a historical linguist — but $\Delta$ stops being the right diagnostic and must be re-estimated per engine.

Ground truth is not random either. TCP keyed a curated subset of ECCO, so $\hat p_v$ inherits that curation and the Horvitz–Thompson fix is only as unbiased as the validation sample. A real hole, not a caveat.

Finally, the humanists have a prior objection I think is correct. Toch, Ifrah and Birnhack's reconstruction of the British Mandate trademark registry from over 300 Gazette editions found a significant date effect on extraction success, skewing the recovered record toward the present — a *coverage* bias sitting on top of everything above and probably larger than it. And Cordell's argument in "Q i-jtb the Raven" goes further: an OCR text is not a degraded surrogate for a true text but a new edition with its own bibliographic history. My framework presupposes a well-defined $f_v$. For eighteenth-century print with unstandardized orthography, where a lexeme appears under several spellings no one at the time called errors, that presupposition is doing real work and may not be earned. The tilt is measurable. What it is a tilt away from is a scholarly construction.

## Further reading

*A note on retrieval: arXiv, ACL Anthology, OUP, Springer, Emerald and most publisher hosts were blocked by this session's egress policy, so the sources below were located and read through search rather than by fetching full texts. Titles, authors, venues and URLs are as retrieved; quantitative figures are as reported in retrieved abstracts and summaries, and the arithmetic I build on them is my own and marked as such.*

- Hill, Hengchen, *Quantifying the impact of dirty OCR on historical text analysis: ECCO as a case study*, Digital Scholarship in the Humanities 34(4):825–843, 2019. [academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/dsh/article-abstract/34/4/825/5476122) — the ECCO-versus-TCP comparison is still the field's only proper paired ground-truth study.
- van Strien, Beelen, Coll Ardanuy, Hosseini, McGillivray, Colavizza, *Assessing the Impact of OCR Quality on Downstream NLP Tasks*, ICAART 2020. [turing.ac.uk](https://www.turing.ac.uk/news/publications/assessing-impact-ocr-quality-downstream-nlp-tasks) — the task-by-task damage report; the harm is consistent but very unequal across tasks.
- Vesalainen, Mäkelä, Ruotsalainen, Tolonen, *Error Patterns in Historical OCR: A Comparative Analysis of TrOCR and a Vision–Language Model*, arXiv:2602.14524, February 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14524) — lower CER bought with silent orthographic normalization; read it before adopting a VLM for a measurement corpus.
- Bourne, Simbeye, Nockels, *The Character Error Vector: Decomposable errors for page-level OCR evaluation*, arXiv:2604.06160, April 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06160v1) — CER is undefined under parsing failure; their three-way decomposition is the metric this area should have had.
- Dell et al., *American Stories: A Large-Scale Structured Text Dataset of Historical U.S. Newspapers*, NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks. [proceedings.neurips.cc](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/ffeb860479ccae44d84c0de32acd693d-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.pdf) — the engine-to-engine CER spread on a fixed sample, which makes the re-OCR argument concrete rather than hypothetical.
- Traub, van Ossenbruggen, Hardman, *Impact Analysis of OCR Quality on Research Tasks in Digital Archives*, TPDL 2015. [link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-24592-8_19) — historians know the bias is there and cannot quantify it; ten years on the diagnostic gap is unchanged.
- Toch, Ifrah, Birnhack, *Temporal bias in historical newspaper digitisation*, Journal of Documentation, 2026. [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1108/JD-07-2025-0196) — extraction success rising toward the present across a 26-year Gazette run.
- Cordell, *"Q i-jtb the Raven": Taking Dirty OCR Seriously*, Book History 20(1):188–225, 2017. [muse.jhu.edu](https://muse.jhu.edu/article/674968/summary) — OCR output as a new edition rather than a corrupted copy; the strongest objection to treating any of this as pure estimation.
- Kanerva, Ledins, Käpyaho, Ginter, *OCR Error Post-Correction with LLMs in Historical Documents: No Free Lunches*, RESOURCEFUL 2025. [aclanthology.org](https://aclanthology.org/2025.resourceful-1.8/) — English improves, Finnish does not reach usable quality. Correction that works unevenly is differential error you introduced yourself.
- *ICDAR 2026 HIPE-OCRepair Competition on LLM-Assisted OCR Post-Correction for Historical Documents*, arXiv:2607.08143. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08143) — read it for the metric design: normalizing away orthographic variation, and a preference score introduced because aggregate error rates mask inconsistency.
- Egami, Hinck, Stewart, Wei, *Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference: Design-based Supervised Learning*, NeurIPS 2023. [naokiegami.com](https://naokiegami.com/paper/dsl.pdf) — the right machinery for cheap-labels-plus-gold-subsample, directly transplantable to keyed transcription samples.
- Cook, Stefanski, *Simulation-extrapolation estimation in parametric measurement error models*, JASA 89(428):1314–1328, 1994; accessible introduction in R News. [journal.r-project.org](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RN-2006-031/RN-2006-031.pdf) — SIMEX, which text is unusually well placed to use because the corruption channel can be simulated.
